item.title: Ather Turns Profitable In Q2, Posts ₹1.3 Cr PAT
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: EV maker Ather Energy turned profitable in the September quarter of FY27, reporting a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr…
item.content:encoded:
EV maker Ather Energy turned profitable in the September quarter of FY27, reporting a consolidated net profit of ₹1.3 Cr against a net loss of ₹154.1 Cr in the corresponding quarter last year.

The company had reported a net loss of ₹51.1 Cr in the preceding June quarter.

Operating revenue surged 62.9% to ₹1,464.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 from ₹898.9 Cr a year earlier. On a sequential basis, revenue increased 20.3% from ₹1,216.9 Cr.

Including other income of ₹62.7 Cr, Ather’s total income stood at ₹1,527 Cr during the quarter, compared with ₹940.7 Cr a year earlier.

While the company turned profitable, other income remained crucial to the outcome. Its operating revenue was ₹61.5 Cr lower than total expenses during the quarter. 

The company earns a bulk of its revenue from vehicle sales. However, revenue from non-vehicle sources including AtherStack Pro, Ather Grid, accessories, spares and servicing rose to 15% of operating revenue, from 12% in the previous year quarter.

Ather turning EBITDA positive in Q1 FY27, when it reported an EBITDA of ₹9 Cr while remaining in the red at the net level. Its EBITDA in Q2 stood at ₹74.2 Cr, with an EBITDA margin of 4.9%, improving from 0.8% in the quarter-ago period. 

In the quarter under review, Ather’s total expenses increased 39.4% to ₹1,526 Cr from ₹1,094.7 Cr, growing slower than its operating revenue.

Ather To Expand Manufacturing Capacity

Alongside its earnings, Ather announced plans to invest ₹122 Cr to bolster its manufacturing capability. With the investment, it plans to add a combined 2.25 Lakh units of annual manufacturing capacity across its Hosur factory and its upcoming Factory 3.0 at Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar. 

Of this, Ather will invest up to ₹58 Cr, including taxes, to bolster manufacturing capacity at its Hosur plant, where existing annual capacity stands at 4.2 Lakh units. The facility operates at 98% capacity utilisation during peak production. The EV maker plans to add capacity for 75,000 units annually at this facility by December 2026.

The investment also includes ₹53 Cr for a new battery line, which is expected to be completed by Q3 FY28.

For its Factory 3.0, Ather is lining up an ₹64 Cr investment to add 1.5 Lakh units of annual capacity over the planned 5 Lakh units. This addition is expected to be completed by Q2 FY28. The first phase of Factory 3.0 is expected to be operationalised by Q3 FY27 and support production of the company’s upcoming EL range line of electric scooters.

Both investments will be financed through a combination of debt and internal accruals. Ather said the expansion would help increase manufacturing output to meet business demand.

During the September quarter, the company raised ₹1,300 Cr through a qualified institutions placement and another ₹200 Cr through a preferential equity allotment. 

The planned expansion comes as Ather said customer enquiries surged 109% YoY to around 10 Lakh, while pre-orders more than doubled to 1.8 Lakh in Q2 FY27. Meanwhile, sales during the quarter stood at 93,211 units, up 42% YoY. 

During the quarter, Ather also jumped on the bandwagon by launching its sub-₹1 Lakh KONARC e-scooter range, taking its portfolio to 15 variants across three product lines. 

Shares of Ather Energy closed 13.7% higher at ₹1,574 apiece on the BSE today.

item.title: L Catterton Invests In InMobi-Backed AI Shopping Platform Glance
item.dc:creator: Anne Florentyna
item.description: Consumer-focused investment firm L Catterton has made a strategic investment in InMobi-backed AI shopping platform Glance to support its expansion,…

item.content:encoded:
Consumer-focused investment firm L Catterton has made a strategic investment in InMobi-backed AI shopping platform Glance to support its expansion, with a particular focus on the US.

The companies did not disclose the investment amount or other transaction terms. Sources told Inc42 that the investment was a fresh equity infusion 

L Catterton said it will use its consumer and category expertise, operating capabilities, and global network to support Glance’s growth.

Glance uses agentic AI to understand consumers’ interests and preferences and recommend products across smartphones, connected TVs, and other digital platforms. It aims to help users move from product discovery to purchase on devices they already use.

Through partnerships with Samsung, Motorola, and DIRECTV, the platform is already available on millions of devices across the US.

Glance founder and CEO Naveen Tewari said the investment validates the company’s approach to shopping, which aims to move commerce beyond search towards agentic shopping.

L Catterton global CEO Scott Dahnke said Glance combines a differentiated shopping proposition with broad distribution across the screens consumers use throughout the day.

From Content To Commerce

Founded in 2019 by InMobi’s four cofounders — Naveen Tewari, Piyush Shah, Abhay Singhal, and Mohit Saxena — Glance initially curated content on smartphone lock screens.

Its original offering had built a user base of 300-400 Mn as of May 2025 without a separate app and attracted around $500 Mn from investors, including Google, Mithril Capital, and Jio Platforms.



Its move into AI shopping took shape publicly in April 2025, when president and COO Piyush Shah previewed the offering at Inc42’s ‘The GenAI Summit’. Shah demonstrated how users could upload a selfie to generate images of themselves wearing different outfits.

Glance subsequently launched its generative AI shopping app in India in May 2025, following a soft launch in the US. Users could visualise themselves in suggested outfits, save the images as wallpapers, or proceed to purchase.

At the time, Glance described three technology layers: a commerce model for discovery and recommendations, a generative AI model for visual experiences, and a transaction model to enable purchases. It had also partnered with Myntra in India and brands in the US to facilitate shopping.

item.title: [Update] IRDAI Extends Feedback Deadline For Insurance Distribution Reforms To Oct 31
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Update | October 26, 12:52 IST The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the deadline for…
item.content:encoded:
Update | October 26, 12:52 IST

The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (IRDAI) has extended the deadline for stakeholders to submit feedback on its proposed insurance distribution reforms to October 31 from October 25, following an “encouraging response” to the consultation paper.

The insurance regulator said it has received more than 650 comments on its consultation paper, titled ‘Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution’, released on September 23. The paper proposes changes to commission structures for insurance distributors and expense limits for insurers.

“In view of the significant interest and to facilitate wider participation, the last date for submission of comments has been extended till 31st October 2026,” IRDAI said.

The extension comes amid opposition from insurance brokers over the proposed changes, with the Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) previously seeking an extension of the feedback deadline until December 31, 2026.

Original | October 7, 12:14 IST

The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) has said that the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (IRDAI) recently proposed norms could trigger a 60-70% revenue collapse across the insurance broking sector. 

Addressing a press briefing, the industry body representatives also said that the insurance distribution sector, which employs over 83 Lakh people, could see the loss of up to 10 Lakh jobs lost as a result of the economic impact of the proposed policies. 

This comes days after IRDAI proposed reintroducing product-wise commission caps for insurance distributors. The regulator also proposed tighter limits on insurers’ overall expenses over concerns related to disproportionate increases in commissions paid to distributors. 

The industry body has also sought an extension of the deadline to submit feedback on the proposed norms to December-end from October 25 currently. 

While noting that the association supports the regulator’s goal of making insurance more affordable and accessible, the IBAI representatives noted that the proposed sweeping changes threaten small businesses and MSMEs. 

The resulting job losses could impact insurance awareness, policy renewals, assistance to policyholders, and penetration of insurance among underserved communities, the representatives added.

The brokers also countered IRDAI’s data that showed that general insurance premiums sourced through brokers had risen 37% whereas commission payouts zoomed 173% between FY23 and FY27. The industry body argued that the rise in commissions since FY23 largely reflected the reclassification of off-book marketing expenses following regularisation, and did not reflect inflationary pressures on insurance consumers. 

The IBAI also claimed that the entire general insurance industry’s operating expenses averaged around 26.5% of gross premiums as against the mandated limit of 30%. Making its point, the representatives also claimed that policyholders received back ₹84.4 in non-life insurance claim payouts for every ₹100 of premium paid over a five-year period. 

This is more than the global average of 72-75%, demonstrating the efficiency of the market in delivering value, the body’s representatives claimed. 

The industry body said it was ready to work with IRDAI to address specific market anomalies, such as misselling or disproportionate remuneration. It has also submitted formal letters to the Prime Minister’s Office and the Finance Ministry on the matter. 

Notably, the pushback comes as insurtech platforms continue to be up in arms against the proposed norms. Last week, Sanjib Jha, founder of insurtech startup Coverfox, said that the proposal could impact the viability of distributing insurance to rural and low-income borrowers. 

Pune-based insurance broker Quickinsure has also trimmed more than 100 jobs in response to the proposal as its founder Anand Shrikhande projected that the industry would see more than 1 Lakh jobs affected due to the changing economics. 

The news has also triggered a major sell-off in listed insurtech majors PB Fintech, which operates Policybazaar, and Turtlemint over fears that the IRDAI’s new policies would dent their core businesses.

item.title: Unacademy Cofounders Plan ₹700 Cr AI, Deeptech Fund
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: Unacademy cofounders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700 Cr venture capital fund to back AI and deeptech…
item.content:encoded:
Unacademy cofounders Gaurav Munjal and Roman Saini are raising a ₹700 Cr venture capital fund to back AI and deeptech startups, less than two months after upGrad completed the acquisition of the edtech startup. 

Named Longshot Capital, the Category II AIF has secured commitments of around ₹250-300 Cr and is targeting its first close in January 2027, ET reported, citing sources. 

Munjal and Saini declined to comment on the development. 

The Bengaluru-based fund plans to invest in 25-28 startups at the seed and pre-Series A stages, with initial cheques of $500,000 to $1.5 Mn and a targeted ownership stake of 8-12%.

Saini will run Longshot Capital full-time, while Munjal will be involved part-time alongside his role heading Unacademy. Both founders will serve as general partners of the investment firm.

The fund plans to deploy its capital over three years and will invest in India-based startups as well as companies founded by entrepreneurs of Indian origin. Its investment mandate will span AI-led businesses and deeptech segments such as manufacturing, space, defence and robotics, rather than consumer brands and retail businesses, the report said.

The fund will have a lifespan of 10-11 years, allowing it to back businesses with longer gestation periods, particularly in AI and deeptech, according to the report. Its prospective investors include startup founders, family offices and overseas institutions.

The fund formalises more than a decade of angel investing by Munjal and Saini. The two have collectively invested over ₹25 Cr through more than 200 angel cheques in companies including Pine Labs, Dhan, Seekho, Ultrahuman, Snabbit, Swish, STAGE, and Third Wave Coffee.

In August, the duo also invested in Superleap, an AI-native customer relationship management platform.

The proposed fund comes amid growing investor interest in frontier technologies, with Indian AI startups raising $438 Mn across 28 deals in the third quarter of 2026, up 265% YoY. Meanwhile, deeptech startups raised $290 Mn across 28 deals during the same period, up 176% YoY. 

Unacademy Founders’ Second Act 

The move adds Munjal and Saini to a growing group of startup founders transitioning from personal angel investments to institutional fund management.

Snapdeal cofounders Kunal Bahl and Rohit Bansal raised ₹333 Cr in external capital for Titan Capital in 2024. Freshworks founder Girish Mathrubootham cofounded the AI-focused Together Fund, while CaratLane founder Mithun Sacheti joined Singularity Growth as a general partner after his exit. Myntra founder Mukesh Bansal operates venture studio Meraki Labs.

The latest development comes over a month after upGrad acquired Unacademy in an all-stock transaction valuing it at ₹1,955 Cr, more than 90% below its peak valuation of $3.4 Bn in August 2021.

Founded in 2015 by Munjal, Saini and Hemesh Singh, Unacademy started as a YouTube channel before evolving into an online learning platform focused on competitive exam preparation. It raised around $880 Mn from investors including SoftBank, Peak XV Partners, Elevation Capital, General Atlantic, Temasek, and Tiger Global.

The startup became a unicorn in September 2020 and reached its peak valuation of $3.5 Bn in 2021, amid a pandemic-led boom in edtech investments. 

However, the reopening of educational institutions and a slowdown in demand for online learning forced Unacademy to rethink its business strategy. Unacademy undertook multiple rounds of layoffs, cut cash burn and scaled down several verticals as it sought to move towards profitability. It also expanded into offline coaching centres to tap demand for in-person test preparation.

Unacademy subsequently explored acquisition opportunities with multiple players, including Allen Career Institute, K-12 Techno Services and upGrad. Its earlier merger discussions with upGrad fell through over valuation differences before the two companies revived negotiations and signed a term sheet in March. The acquisition was completed in September.

Meanwhile, Munjal, on X yesterday, pushed back on criticism against the risk appetite of Indian deeptech investors, highlighting that startups like Astrobase, Airbound and Sarvam AI have been able to raise large rounds in short time periods. He also noted that consumer tech companies like Groww, Eternal and Meesho, all of whom went public in recent years, have provided “spectacular outcomes”.

item.title: Growth Vs Profitability: Swiggy’s Tug-Of-War
item.dc:creator: Gargi Sarkar
item.description: Swiggy’s results for the second quarter (Q2) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) show that the tug of war between…
item.content:encoded:
Swiggy’s results for the second quarter (Q2) of the financial year 2026-27 (FY27) show that the tug of war between growth and profitability is intensifying, as Instamart’s mounting losses threaten to overshadow the improving performance of its food-delivery business.

On October 23, 2026, the company’s shares fell around 15% to ₹179.90 on the BSE, wiping out roughly ₹9,000 Cr in market capitalisation in a single session. The sell-off came after Swiggy reported its results, with widening losses at Instamart overshadowing improving profitability in its food delivery business. The stock has also lost more than half its value since its market debut in November 2024. 

The company’s revenue from operations increased 36.1% YoY to ₹7,571 Cr in the September quarter. Its consolidated net loss narrowed to ₹922 Cr from ₹1,092 Cr a year earlier, but widened from ₹791 Cr in the preceding quarter. 

The contrast within the business is becoming more pronounced. Food delivery reported record adjusted EBITDA, supported by advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies. Instamart, meanwhile, saw its adjusted EBITDA loss widen to ₹895 Cr from ₹849 Cr a year earlier, even as its net order value (NOV) grew 13.4% sequentially.

This has put investors in a spot, questioning whether Swiggy’s rising investments today can deliver sustainable returns tomorrow. Or will the coming quarters reveal whether Instamart’s renewed growth can translate into better margins? But before that…

Instamart’s Growth Comes At A Cost

Instamart’s Q2 numbers show a recovery in growth momentum, but not yet a corresponding improvement in profitability. The business’s net order value (NOV) rose 13.4% QoQ to ₹6,594 Cr in Q2 FY27 against 2.5% growth in the preceding quarter. Orders rose 29.3% YoY to 130 Mn. Instamart added 1.3 Mn monthly transacting users during the quarter, taking its user base to 14.8 Mn, up 23% YoY.

These are meaningful signs of demand. Management has also pointed to higher order frequency and stronger retention in the earnings call as evidence that Instamart is building shopping habits rather than relying solely on one-off purchases. Its strategy is to deepen engagement through everyday categories such as fresh produce and staples, while using differentiated assortment to give customers reasons to return.

However, customer and order growth are only one side of the story. Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss widened to ₹895 Cr in Q2 FY27, while its contribution margin deteriorated. According to the foodtech’s shareholders’ letter, Instamart reported a contribution margin of -1.0% of gross order value (GOV). The number suggests that the business is still spending heavily to attract and retain customers, fulfil orders and build out its network.

“This creates a difficult trade-off. Promotions and pricing investments can help drive orders, while more stores can improve proximity and delivery speed. But both require capital and operating expenditure. Unless higher order volumes, better monetisation and denser delivery networks improve the economics of each order, growth can continue to increase the absolute loss,” an industry source said.

The Swiggy management believes Instamart’s customer cohorts are becoming more productive and that differentiated assortment can improve retention over time. The company is also working to increase revenue per order through product mix, private labels and advertising, while reducing costs through network densification, automation and operating leverage.

The break-even ambition, however, remains elusive. Management has said Instamart needs to reach roughly 2.3X its current scale, with annualised NOV of around ₹60,000 Cr against approximately ₹26,400 Cr at present, alongside a contribution of about ₹30 per order. Swiggy estimates that roughly two-thirds of the improvement needed would come from higher revenue per order and the remainder from lower costs per order.

This is a roadmap rather than a near-term result. The company has not been able to give a detailed timeline for reaching break-even or quantify how much each lever would contribute. Investors will, therefore, need to look beyond headline growth and track whether contribution margin, order economics and adjusted EBITDA improve together.

Management expects double-digit sequential NOV growth in Q3 and an improvement of around 100 basis points in adjusted EBITDA margin QoQ. This makes the next quarter an important juncture.

Blinkit Raises The Bar For Instamart

Instamart’s challenge is not simply to grow. It has to build a network capable of competing with Blinkit while improving the economics of that expansion.

The difference in store footprint is also considerable. Instamart added 69 net dark stores in Q2 FY27, taking its total to 1,240 across 133 cities. Blinkit added 308 stores during the same quarter, taking its network to 2,751. Blinkit’s network is now more than twice the size of Instamart’s.

Scale matters in quick commerce because it affects how close a platform can be to customers, how efficiently it can fulfil orders and how much volume it can route through its network. A larger footprint can also provide more opportunities to improve availability and spread certain operating costs. But store count alone does not establish which business has better economics: store maturity, order density, basket size, local competition and the cost of operating each location all matter.

The financial contrast in Q2 is also stark. Blinkit reported positive adjusted EBITDA of ₹184 Cr, compared with Instamart’s adjusted EBITDA loss of ₹895 Cr. Blinkit’s NOV grew 22.2% sequentially, ahead of Instamart’s 13.4% growth. 

Eternal’s management has cited store paybacks and lower competitive intensity in Tier II markets, while maintaining its FY29 EBITDA ambition for Blinkit. In contrast, Swiggy has emphasised building customer habits, improving retention and developing its existing Tier I and II network. 

Instamart’s management did not commit to a new accelerated expansion plan in the earnings call, suggesting the near-term focus is on making the existing network more productive rather than simply matching Blinkit store for store.

“There is a reasonable case for this approach. Adding stores without sufficient local demand can dilute returns, and a smaller network can still be productive if it generates enough orders per location. But restraint also carries a risk: a weaker physical footprint can limit reach and availability in a market where speed and convenience are central to the proposition,” the executive quoted above said.

Therefore, the key question is whether Instamart can close the gap through better throughput, assortment and monetisation, rather than relying primarily on expansion. 

Swiggy’s shareholder letter also points to a planned transition to an inventory-led model, under which Instamart would own the inventory it sells. Management expects this to improve contribution margin by around 80 basis points and shorten the working-capital cycle. The transition is expected to begin mid-Q3 FY27 and take two to three quarters to complete.

What Can Support Swiggy’s Valuation?

Swiggy’s market fall also reflects the tension between a relatively stronger food delivery business and a quick commerce operation that continues to consume substantial resources.

Food delivery GOV grew 17.7% YoY to ₹10,054 Cr in Q2 FY27. Adjusted EBITDA increased 42% to ₹341 Cr, with the adjusted EBITDA margin improving to 3.4% from 2.8% a year ago. Higher advertising revenue and delivery efficiencies supported the performance. 

This business provides an important counterweight to Instamart’s losses. Its profitability shows that Swiggy can generate operating earnings from an established marketplace, even as it continues to invest in newer businesses. It also gives the company a base from which to fund growth.

The difficulty is that stronger food-delivery performance has not yet offset the pressure from Instamart. Swiggy’s consolidated net loss widened sequentially, and analysts have questioned whether its quick commerce growth is keeping pace with expectations. 

Citi, for instance, noted that Instamart’s sequential NOV growth was below its estimate, while its adjusted EBITDA loss was higher than expected. CLSA also flagged slower-than-expected growth and wider losses, while other brokerages have lowered price targets amid concerns about execution and the time required to reach profitability. 

This, however, does not mean that Instamart’s growth strategy cannot work. Quick commerce requires upfront investment in stores, inventory, customer acquisition and logistics, and some of those costs may become more efficient as order density improves. The issue is how long investors should be expected to wait for those benefits.

Therefore, Swiggy’s immediate task is to show that Q2 was a turning point in loss trajectory, as management expects, rather than another quarter in which growth came at a higher cost. The next set of results will need to show sustained sequential NOV growth alongside improving contribution and adjusted EBITDA margins. Customer additions will matter, but so will repeat ordering, store productivity and the extent to which revenue per order rises.

The inventory-led transition will be another milestone to watch. For now, as Swiggy continues to get stuck in a tug-of-war between profitability and growth, its market fall is a reminder that revenue growth alone is unlikely to reassure investors.
